I ask everybody I work with the same question at the end of a project, and I have been doing it for about nine years. Not what went wrong, because that question makes people defend themselves and you learn nothing. The question is: if you did this again next month, with the same money, what would you do differently? And the difference in the answers is extraordinary. The first one puts people on trial. The second one makes them curious about their own work. Almost nobody says they would change the big thing. They say they would move one meeting. They say they would have brought the musical director into the room in week one instead of week three. And here is the part that surprised me for the first three years: if you collect twenty of those answers across twenty projects, you do not get twenty different problems. You get the same four, described by different people who all think they are the only one who noticed.

There is a trap in the hypothetical, and I fell into it for years, so let me name it. It is very satisfying to describe the perfect version of the job. If I had three more days. If the room were bigger. If somebody else had made that decision in two thousand nineteen. All of that is true, and none of it is useful on its own, because the room is the size it is and the decision was made. What changed things for me was one extra sentence, and I learned it from somebody who ran a studio for thirty years. She would listen to the whole beautiful description of the perfect version, and then she would say: fine, now what is the cheapest half of that? And there always is a cheapest half. If you want two extra days of rehearsal, you are not getting them. But the reason you want them is usually one specific thing, and that thing might cost four hours on a Tuesday. Describe the perfect version so that you can find the affordable piece of it. Do not describe it so that you can be right about what you were never going to get.

Pedro says that if he had a clean slate, he would not rebuild the whole system. He explains that he would change two decisions that were made in the first month. He says that if the budget were bigger, he would hire a second engineer for the live week. He adds that realistically nobody gets a clean slate, and that he is stuck with three constraints. He says that what he would trade for is four hours of rehearsal in the right place. Then he asks the other person what they would do differently.
